 The K-drama streaming on HBO Max explores South Korea’s patriarchy through sex toys, but struggles to deliver on its provocative premise
 3 -MIN READ 3 -MIN Listen Pierce Conran in Seoul Published: 9:15pm, 22 Oct 2026 Lead cast: Nam Ji-hyun, Kim Jae-young
 South Korea finds itself at an interesting juncture in its social evolution in the mid-2020s. Following the success of works such as the 2016 book Kim Ji-young, Born 1982 and its hit 2019 film adaptation , which brought the country’s gender inequality into sharp focus, the imbalance remains stubbornly stark. People now recognise this imbalance and are unafraid to label it for what it is – “patriarchy” is no longer a dirty word. Yet change has been slow. South Korea’s rapid economic advance is one of the modern age’s great national success stories, but its social progress, which moves only as fast as generational change, could never hope to match it.
 Over time, this has led to a societal schism particularly pronounced in a media landscape swerving between gruelling social awareness stories and luminous metropolises filled with beautiful fashionistas.
